title: Instruction-Level Parallelism
summary: How a single core runs more than one instruction at a time — and why that speedup eventually hits a wall.

blocks.markdown:
**Instruction-level parallelism (ILP)** is running more than one instruction at the same time within a single core.

- Basic [pipelining](pipelining) overlaps instruction *stages*; ILP goes further and overlaps whole *instructions*.
- Needs extra hardware: multiple pipelines, reordering logic, and prediction.
- The payoff is limited — real programs only offer so much independent work.

blocks.subTitle: Superscalar
blocks.markdown:
A **superscalar** CPU has more than one execution pipeline, so it can start several instructions in the same clock cycle.

- **Issue width** is how many instructions it can dispatch per cycle (e.g. 4-wide).
- One pipeline finishes about one instruction per cycle at best; N pipelines aim for close to N.
- Real speedup is always less than N — instructions depend on each other.

blocks.subTitle: In-order vs out-of-order
blocks.markdown:
Two ways to schedule instructions once they're fetched.

| | In-order | Out-of-order (OoO) |
|---|---|---|
| Runs instructions | Strictly as written | Whichever is ready first |
| Stalls on | Any instruction not ready | Only if nothing is ready |
| Hardware cost | Simple | Complex (extra tracking) |

OoO keeps pipelines busy by skipping a stalled instruction and running a later, ready one instead.

blocks.subTitle: Why order breaks things
blocks.markdown:
Running out of order is only safe if results still come out **as if** the program ran in order.

- A **dependency** is when one instruction needs another's result before it can run.
- OoO hardware tracks these and only runs an instruction once its inputs are ready.
- Two instructions with no dependency between them can freely run in either order, or together.

blocks.subTitle: The false-dependency problem
blocks.markdown:
Reusing the same register name can create a dependency that isn't a *real* one.

- **WAR (write-after-read)** — a later instruction writes a register before an earlier one has read it.
- **WAW (write-after-write)** — two instructions write the same register, and order must be preserved.
- Both come from **running out of registers to name**, not from actual data flow.

blocks.subTitle: The fix
blocks.markdown:
**Register renaming** gives each write a fresh, hidden physical register, so instructions stop colliding on the same name.

- The visible register names (like `R1`) map to a larger pool of **physical registers** under the hood.
- This removes WAR and WAW hazards entirely — only true data dependencies remain.
- It's what makes aggressive out-of-order execution practical.

blocks.subTitle: The reorder buffer
blocks.markdown:
Instructions may *finish* out of order, but the program's visible effects must land **in order**.

- The **reorder buffer (ROB)** holds finished instructions until it's their turn to **commit** (become permanent, in original program order).
- If an earlier instruction hasn't committed yet, later ones wait in the ROB even if already done.
- Commit-in-order is what lets the CPU undo work cleanly after a mistake.

**Speculative execution** means running instructions past a branch before knowing which way it goes, using a guess from [branch-prediction](branch-prediction).

- Guessed-right work commits normally — free performance.
- Guessed-wrong work is thrown away; the ROB discards it since it never commits.
- Deep pipelines with wide issue rely on speculation, or they'd stall constantly at branches.

Fetch and decode stay in order; renaming removes false dependencies; issue and execute go out of order; the ROB restores order at commit.

ILP can't grow forever — this ceiling is called the **ILP wall**.

- **True dependencies** in the code set a hard floor on how much can overlap.
- Branches are frequent, so speculation misses cost real cycles.
- Wider issue and bigger ROBs give shrinking returns while burning more power and chip area.

This is a major reason CPUs shifted toward [multicore-multiprocessing](multicore-multiprocessing) instead of ever-wider single cores.

Common mistakes:

- **"Out-of-order means results come out in any order."** No — only execution timing changes; commit is always in order.
- **"More pipelines always means proportional speedup."** No — dependencies and branches cap real gains far below the issue width.
- **"Speculation is free."** Wrong guesses cost the wasted work plus a pipeline flush.

blocks.subTitle: What is ILP
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is instruction-level parallelism?**

Executing multiple instructions at once within a single core, instead of one at a time. Achieved through superscalar issue (multiple pipelines) and out-of-order execution, bounded by real dependencies in the code.

blocks.subTitle: In-order vs out-of-order
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain in-order vs out-of-order execution.**

In-order runs instructions exactly as written and stalls the whole pipeline when one isn't ready. Out-of-order runs whichever ready instruction comes next, tracks dependencies in hardware, and still commits results in original order via the reorder buffer.

blocks.subTitle: What limits ILP
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What ultimately limits how much ILP you can extract?**

True data dependencies between instructions, branch frequency and misprediction cost, and diminishing returns from wider issue and larger reorder buffers — collectively called the ILP wall. It's why chip designers turned to multiple cores instead of pushing single-core ILP further.
